doc.title: Howard Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2025

title: Richter tuning, bends and modes explained
summary: With demonstrations, Levy explains the Richter tuning, bends, modal positions, and his overblows and overdraws making it chromatic.

blocks.x: You know the first time I saw on a date, it was a blues date, and I had never seen the harmonica. This particular player had a whole tacklebox full of these harps. And I was like holy cow, you have to have one for – you know they had to have one for every key.
I guess you don’t have to carry a tacklebox around with you?

Well I do carry a bunch of different keys because well basically, and just for the sake of demonstrating, I’m just going to use the C harp. I mean it’s not my favorite harmonica but it’s the universal key of the white keys of the piano. And basically what the Germans did in the 1820s or 1830s or whenever this tuning system was figured out, this one probably came about in the 1850s. It’s call the Richter tuning. And they tried to design this instrument so it could play the one and the five chord on the bottom [demonstrates], and the melody notes in the middle [demonstrates] and then to keep going until they ran out of notes up on the top. It’s very precise. So they left out a bunch of notes in the first octave, to be able to just have the [demonstrates] that five chord [demonstrates] and in the middle [demonstrates] you have all the notes of the major scale. So basically the folk music played on this instrument, you know, [demonstrates] they could harmonize, that was the idea. It’s like an autoharp. You have like the one and the five chord. And so if you play [demonstrates] if you reverse that breathing pattern and start on the inhale [demonstrates] you get the Mixolydian mode and you get a blues shuffle. And then, as if by magic, all these bent notes – am I distorting the mic at all?

That stuff, the Germans had no idea they were designing that. Because what happens is, and I’m not going to get too geeky here, but you can bend the higher note on a hole down to just above the pitch of the lower note. And since they left out a whole bunch of notes on the bottom octave [demonstrates] you’ve got all that [demonstrates]. So you have almost the complete chromatic scale on the first octave, just [demonstrates]. There’s a few things missing, and in the middle octave you get more notes – there’s a bunch more notes missing that you can’t get by bends. But I’m going to get – I’ll explain a little more of that but basically what you have here is you have a modal instrument. So you can play in C major [demonstrates]; G Mixolydian [demonstrates] with bends, whatever; you can

play in D Dorian [demonstrates]; and you can play in A Aeolian [demonstrates] whoops I made that Dorian, sorry [demonstrates]; and you can play in E Phrygian [demonstrates]. So you can hear all these flavors that are in there. “Gee that doesn’t sound like a harmonica.” That’s because 99 percent of the time you hear guys going [demonstrates]. They’re only playing in what’s called second position, which is Mixolydian mode with all the bends and stuff. And then you’ve got Locrian mode on the B [demonstrates]. So those are the modal positions. In the harmonica world they call them by numbers that correspond to the fifths of the circle of fifths. And of course I came along and figured out how to get the missing notes [demonstrates] with a thing called overblows and overdraws, and made it into a chromatic instrument. And I can play like pretty much anything in any key except I can’t go [demonstrates] I can’t do that in every key on one harmonica because that is like the innate structure of the instrument that allows you to do that. So if I want to play a traditional blues in D let’s say, I’d need a G harmonica to play the Mixolydian mode you know. So anyway that’s a little bit of the –
